extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (Office personnel) and patent practitioners reviewing MPEP guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Procedure and substantive standards for determining whether a patent specification provides an adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph). Covers examiner methodology, claim-by-claim analysis, evidence of possession, species/genus distinction, means‑plus‑function support, and factors to consider by art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental written description inquiry (possession)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a question of fact determined case-by-case. Examiner should consider whether the disclosure shows applicant had possession of the claimed subject matter at filing (e.g., Vas-Cath, AbbVie/Janssen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner methodology and burden (prima facie case)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description is present; the examiner has the initial burden, after a thorough reading and evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize the written description as providing adequate support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a prima facie case the examiner must identify claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the disclosure fails (e.g., Hyatt v. Dudas). If made, burden shifts to applicant to point out support or amend claims. A simple explicit statement may sometimes suffice for amended claims (see MPEP §2163.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: For amended or newly added claims show support in original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; if applicant points out where/ how the originally filed disclosure supports the amendment(s) the examiner must then present reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize such support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple statement such as 'applicant has not pointed out where the new claim is supported' may be sufficient where support is not apparent. See Hyatt v. Dudas and MPEP §§714.02, 2163.04, 2163.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and whole-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given a reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the entire claim (preamble, transitional phrase, body) must be considered in assessing written description support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is essential to the written description analysis; preamble language and transitional terms (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') affect scope and must be evaluated (see Genentech, PPG, Pac-Tec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of transitional phrases ('comprising' / 'consisting essentially of')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' is open-ended (covers recited subject matter alone or in combination with unrecited matter). 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground, admitting unlisted ingredients that do not materially affect the basic and novel properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent clear specification disclosure of what the basic and novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' may be treated as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art purposes. Applicant bears burden to show additional components would not materially change characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of definitions or details of well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis for a written description rejection, but examiners must avoid reading specification-only limitations into claim scope (see Bell Comm., Corning Glass Works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review entire application for support (embodiments, figures, sequence listings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before determining adequacy of written description, examiner should review claims and entire specification including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings to understand how applicant provides support for claimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information well known in the art need not be described in detail, but sufficient information must be provided to show possession of the invention. Consider field of invention and level of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice or detailed disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, detailed drawings, or structural chemical formulas that permit a person skilled in the art to recognize applicant had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice (constructing an embodiment or performing a process with all claim limitations) is strong evidence, but not always necessary. Drawings alone can provide sufficient written description in appropriate cases (Vas-Cath, Wolfensperger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession may be shown by identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description may be shown by disclosure of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics (e.g., partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with structure) so a skilled artisan recognizes possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For biotechnology, function-plus-minimal-structure can suffice when there is a well-established correlation between structure and function. Examples include sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length; deposits may support biological material claims (37 CFR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only disclosure generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing a composition or molecule by its function alone typically will not suffice to describe the composition adequately unless a well-established correlation between function and structure exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function-only descriptions are 'little more than a wish' without enabling identification of the claimed subject matter (see Eli Lilly, Fiers, Amgen). For antibodies/biomolecules, claims defined only by binding affinity to an inadequately described antigen may fail (Noelle v. Lederman, Centocor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for biological/material deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposits made after filing may be relied on to support correction of sequence information only if applicant submits a statement in compliance with 37 CFR 1.804 stating the deposited biological material is the biological material specifically defined in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description of actual reduction to practice of a biological material may be shown by specifically describing a deposit made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq., especially 1.804 and 1.809.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑(or step‑)plus‑function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof; the written description must adequately link particular structure/materials/acts to perform the claimed function or be clear such structures are known to skilled artisans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider the specification, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Mere assertion that skilled artisans would know the structures is insufficient; lack of corresponding structure may render the claim both indefinite under 112(b) and lacking written description under 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species versus genus analysis and appropriate disclosure level
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is treated accordingly; a claim encompassing multiple embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus. The required description level varies with the invention's nature and the state of knowledge in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For single-species claims, examiner should determine (A) whether application describes an actual reduction to practice, (B) whether drawings or structural formulas show completeness, or (C) whether identifying characteristics suffice. For genera, more disclosure may be needed depending on predictability of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for single-embodiment/species claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is drawn to a single embodiment/species, determine: (A) whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, whether drawings/structural formulas sufficiently show invention as whole; (C) if not, whether identifying characteristics are sufficiently detailed to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If complete structure (or acts) is disclosed, written description satisfied. If not, consider whether other identifying characteristics (structure-function correlation, partial structure, methods of making) would lead a skilled artisan to conclude possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (with known correlation to structure), and methods of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on prior patents and literature helps determine art maturity. In mature arts less disclosure may be required; in unpredictable/emerging arts more evidence is needed. The analysis is factual and depends on the invention and state of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between skill level and required specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often an inverse correlation between the level of skill/knowledge in the art and the specificity of disclosure necessary to satisfy written description; more mature arts may require less detail, unpredictable arts require more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature technologies, written description questions should not be raised for claims present in the original application even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to reject for lack of written description versus enablement or indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim omitting matter disclosed as essential in the specification may be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), 112(b) (indefiniteness), or pre-AIA equivalents; rejection under 112(b) cannot stand where the specification satisfies 112(a) for means-plus-function recitations not challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a means‑plus‑function claim lacks corresponding structure the claim may be indefinite under 112(b) and also lack adequate written description under 112(a). Examiners should consider interplay between these grounds and treat each limitation accordingly (see In re Noll, Aristocrat, Atmel).
